Tissue Regeneration

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A scientist uses Zebra fish hearts to repair human hearts

Unique Selling Point:
This is groundbreaking new medical research published in Nov 2016.

Summary:
Pitt researcher uses zebrafish to help mammalian hearts regenerate, including promising results in human heart cells in vitro. Many lower forms of life on earth exhibit an extraordinary ability to regenerate tissue, limbs, and even organs—a skill that is lost among humans and other mammals. Now, a University of Pittsburgh researcher has used the components of the cellular “scaffolding” of a zebrafish to regenerate heart tissues in mammals, specifically mice, as well as exhibiting promising results in human heart cells in vitro.

Further information:
How Do You Mend a Broken Heart?

Pitt researcher uses zebrafish to help mammalian hearts regenerate, including promising results in human heart cells in vitro. Many lower forms of life on earth exhibit an extraordinary ability to regenerate tissue, limbs, and even organs—a skill that is lost among humans and other mammals. Now, a University of Pittsburgh researcher has used the components of the cellular “scaffolding” of a zebrafish to regenerate heart tissues in mammals, specifically mice, as well as exhibiting promising results in human heart cells in vitro.

The findings offer promise to overcoming heart disease, the leading cause of death for men and women.

The study, led by Yadong Wang, the William Kepler Whiteford Professor in Bioengineering in the Swanson School of Engineering and the principal investigator of the Biomaterials Foundry at Pitt, found that a single administration of extracellular matrices (ECM) from zebrafish hearts restored the function of the heart and regenerated adult mouse heart tissues after acute myocardial infarction.

“The heart beats as if nothing has happened to it,” said Wang. “And our approach is really simple.”

The study also found that the zebrafish ECM protected human cardiac myocytes—specialized cells that form heart muscle—from stresses.

ECM are the architectural foundations of tissues and organs; not only do they provide a “scaffolding” on which cells can grow and migrate, they assist in the signaling necessary for the organ to develop, grow, or regenerate.

In mammals, the heart quickly loses the ability to regenerate after the organism is born, except for a brief period after birth. In lower animals, such as zebrafish, the heart retains that ability throughout their lives: up to 20 percent of a zebrafish’s heart can be damaged or removed, and within days the heart’s capacity has been fully restored.

Wang and his team first separated the ECM from the cells so that the recipient heart would not reject the treatment. They did this by freezing the zebrafish cardiac tissue, causing the cell membranes to burst and allowing the researchers to retrieve the ECM, a process called decellularization. Wang noted that he and his colleagues are among the first to decellularize non-mammalian tissues for applications in regenerative medicine. They then injected the ECM into the hearts of mice with damaged heart muscles and watched the hearts repair themselves.

“It’s difficult to inject foreign cells into a body because the body will recognize them as foreign and reject them; that’s not the case with ECM,” said Wang. Wang explained that, because ECMs are composed of collagen, elastin, carbohydrates and signaling molecules and have no cell surface markers, DNA or RNA from the donor, the recipient is less likely to reject the treatment.

Wang said that restored function starts almost immediately, and healing is noticeable as early as five days after treatment; within a week, his team could see the heart beating more strongly than the hearts of the untreated animals.

The researchers tested the effectiveness of ECM from normal zebrafish and from zebrafish with damaged hearts, in which the ECM had already begun the healing process. They found that while both types of ECM were effective in repairing damage to the mice hearts, the ECM obtained from the zebrafish hearts that were healing were even more potent in restoring heart function in the mice.

Wang is now working on a process to regenerate nerves in mammals using the same process and hopes to expand the heart treatments to larger animals in a future study.

The study “Decellularized zebrafish cardiac extracellular matrix induces mammalian heart regeneration” was published in the Nov. 18 issue of Science Advances.

The work was funded in part by the American Heart Association and National Institutes of Health.

Press Release:


Tissue Regeneration
Can scientists mend a broken heart? New medical research on the zebra-fish could hold the answer. This tiny freshwater fish has an amazing
ability to regenerate its own heart, spinal cord and other tissue and this could offer hope of recovery to millions of people living with permanent
heart damage after a heart attack. Carte Blanche examines this medical discovery.

Script:


V/O:
These are zebrafish. Not only are they a popular species in freshwater aquariums, but they are also responsible for an amazing medical breakthrough.
LINK:
These tiny creatures could in future be instrumental in saving the lives of millions of heart attack victims. It is because this fish has a heart with astounding regenerative capabilities.
Prof Yadong Wang:
You can actually cut about twenty percent of the heart off and it will regenerate. If you look at the heart, maybe a month after you cut off a significant chunk of it, it looks the same as a healthy heart. It regenerates muscle.
V/O:
Prof Yadong Wang of the University of Pittsburgh is a bioengineer with a special interest in regenerative medicine. He says the zebrafish’s ability to regenerate organs and tissue is astounding.
Yadong:
Zebrafish can definitely regenerate other muscle. A lot of its own tissue it can regenerate very well. Like a fin. A fin is almost like an arm. It’s not the same but it has bones and so on. It can regenerate that.
V/O:
It can even regenerate a spinal cord. Here is a zebrafish with a section of its spinal cord missing being subjected to a water current– it can hardly move.

But after a few days, the spinal cord has grown back completely. And this is the same fish – fully functional.
LINK 2:
This ability of the Zebra fish and other animals to regenerate tissue is unfortunately not shared by humans. And it is a pity especially in cases where crucial tissues like heart muscle is damaged.
V/O
And heart muscle usually gets damaged during a heart attack.
Dr Mogaladi
You get a heart attack when you have insufficient blood supply to the muscle. An area of heart muscle gets a cut-off of blood supply and dies off. If it dies, the heart stops functioning and if it is a larger area the remaining functioning part cannot sustain life and a person might die from that.
V/O:
Dr Shungu Mogaladi is the head of Cardiothoracic Surgery at the University of The Witwatersrand and Charlotte Maxeke Academic Hospital. He says if parts of the heart muscle have died off, the damage is permanent.
Mogaladi:
The dead muscle does not recover. It forms a scar tissue.
V/O:
When a part of your heart muscle has died off in this way, and your heart is not functioning properly it has serious consequences for your health and general day to day living.
Mogaladi:
When a person has a larger area of damaged heart muscle, that cannot give adequate blood flow and a person is persistently in heart failure. You cannot breathe properly, you cannot walk, you cannot work, and you cannot do your daily chores.
LINK 3:
So once the heart’s muscle has been damaged, what can modern medicine offer to patients in terms of treatment?
Yadong:
So actually we do not have too much. Once you have a heart attack the first order of business is to get the blood flow back to the tissue. So you stent or you do bypass surgery. After that you can manage the pressure, beta blocker and so on. You essentially calm down the body so the heart does not work so hard. After that you do not have too much other choice.
V/O:
The only other option is a heart transplant, but there are few donors and many people die while waiting for a new heart.

Prof Wang decided to approach the issue by thinking out of the box. And the zebrafish intrigued him. Modern science does not yet understand the mechanisms or genes involved in the regenerative process, but that did not deter him.
Yadong:
I heard about the amazing capability to regenerate of the Zebra fish. And I thought how come we do not have that. What caused the difference and other people are studying it already. So as a bio-engineer, instead of studying the mechanism of why zebra fish regenerate like that, I said "Ok maybe we can use that." Maybe we can use that mechanism even without knowing what it is for yourself. To benefit human cardiac regeneration.
LINK 4:
He wanted to see if he could induce human hearts to regenerate like Zebrafish hearts. It was uncharted waters but he knew that on a genetic level humans and Zebrafish are closely related.
Yadong:
About 90% of the genes are the same. A lot of the proteins that work in the fish is the same and will work in us as well. And vice versa. Like a lot of our proteins will work in the fish. It might not be a hundred percent efficiency but it will work.
V/O:
Prof Wang decided to introduce some components of the zebrafish heart tissue into human hearts to see if that would have any effect.
Yadong:
If you think about the tissue generally you have two components. You have the cell and you have the matrix outside the cell. We call it the ECM, Extra Cellular Matrix. We cannot take the cell directly because our body will reject it. It is not our cell, it is a foreign cell so you will reject that. But the matrix - we will not reject that. So I thought maybe because the matrix is an integral part of regeneration we can probably take that Extra Cellular Matrix from the zebra fish and help our heart to regenerate.
V/O:
So he wanted to introduce extra cellular matrices of zebrafish directly into damaged heart muscle. But he could not start with human hearts. So he turned to other mammalian hearts – mice hearts.
LINK 5:
They induced a heart attack in the mice so that the mice hearts would have the same damage human heart would have after a severe heart attack.

But how do you get the extra cellular matrices into mouse heart muscle?
Yadong:
The Zebrafish heart is very very small. It is very very thin tissue. Only about three or four cell layers thick so you are talking about…. I would say 100 micron or so. Very thin tissue. So all we did is to freeze the heart, cut into small pieces and use a few enzymes to remove the nuclear contents and that is it.
V/O:
After they washed out the cellular content all that remained were the extracellular matrices seen here under an electron microscope. This they ground into a very fine powder.
Yadong:
Then we inject that powder into the heart. It is very very fine, nanometres fine so we can inject it very easy with a very thin needle.
V/O:
The results were amazing.
Yadong:
So when we injected it into the mice we noticed a few different things. One is the heart is pumping more efficiently, two the ventricle is not so thin, it is a little thicker. Three, we don’t see as much scar tissue.
V/O:
So zebrafish heart matrices made the mice hearts regenerate to a large extent.
LINK 6:
If the same effect can be induced in humans with damaged hearts, it would mean that millions of lives will be saved.
Yadong:
It is a very simple process but we are working with other investigators of the University of Pittsburg to look at what component of that matrix might contribute to the effect.
V/O:
As a cardiac specialist Dr Mogaladi is excited about the possibilities that Prof Wang’s work could offer.
Mogaladi:
There are a lot of patients walking around with end stage heart failure. And we don’t meet the requirements that are needed with heart transplants in the country. So the Zebrafish can provide another platform in helping people who are actually in waiting for a heart transplant.
V/O:
However, Prof Wang warns that it could take up to five years before the procedure could be approved for human trials.
LINK 7:
The next step would be to do the experiments in large animals to see if the tiny fish could also work its magic on that level as well, and Prof Wang is cautiously optimistic.
Yadong:
I hope this can be a product that can save someone’s life. And I will be very, very happy if that happens.
